content:
Bloomberg yesterday published a report stating that Apple is about to launch a brand new "Apple Upgrade" rental contract to replace the existing "iPhone Upgrade Program".

There appear to be two major differences between the two, and one of them could be quite concerning...

The way the "iPhone Upgrade Program" works is fairly straightforward. The purchase cost is spread over 24 months, and once the two-year contract period expires, you own the device outright, with no credit charges during that period.

(In addition, you also have the option to upgrade to a new iPhone after 12 months. In such cases, a new two-year contract begins, and you essentially sell the old device back to Apple using the amount you have already paid.)

Apple has yet to make any official announcement regarding the new plan, so we cannot determine exactly how it will work. However, according to Bloomberg, the new plan will cover most other Apple products, while the lease term for Mac products will be three years. So far, things seem reasonable.

But the concerning part is that the report suggests the new plan will operate quite similarly to a car lease. Under this type of contract, you are not paying the full price of the product over the lease term; instead, the monthly payments only cover the depreciation of the product during the lease period, along with any interest charges. Once the lease expires, you do not own the product — you are essentially just renting it.

Similarly, assuming it works like a car lease, you must return the product when the lease expires, or pay a large "balloon payment" to cover the difference between the depreciation amount and the original price of the product.

Of course, this means the monthly payments will be lower than those of the current plan. Some may view this as a good thing, as it would make Apple products more affordable for more people.

However, what is concerning is that most people will not set aside an additional amount each month in order to pay that balloon payment at the end of the lease. The most common outcome when a car lease ends is that people return the old car and then sign a new lease. Essentially, they are trapped in a never-ending cycle, never truly owning the product.

If the new Apple Upgrade plan follows the same model, the situation will be identical. Consumers who purchase products in this way will essentially be forced to upgrade their iPhone every two years, or their Mac every three years, without the option to continue using their existing device for many years. Even disregarding interest charges, the overall cost of ownership of the product will increase significantly in the long run.

Furthermore, if the report is accurate, the new plan does not include AppleCare+, and users could find themselves in a situation where the device is lost, stolen, or severely damaged beyond repair during the lease term. Not only would they have to continue making monthly payments for a device they have already lost, but they would also need to pay the balloon payment at the end of the lease.

I can understand Apple's desire to streamline operations by introducing a single upgrade plan and therefore withdrawing the existing one. But I believe a more consumer-friendly approach would be to offer plans that allow people to choose for themselves, enjoying credit benefits while also having control over how frequently they upgrade.

What are your thoughts on this? Feel free to share your opinions in the comments section.
